notes:
I couldn't find anything on vv. 39–42 in what I read, and I found nothing from oca.org, the Lutheran sites or any Pentecostal or charismatic site. The NET Bible page loaded only up to note 34, so its notes for vv. 22–42 are not included.

**v. 22**
- **The feast.** Adam Clarke says Judas Maccabeus started this feast to remember cleansing the temple after Antiochus Epiphanes defiled it. It began on 25 Kislev and lasted eight days. Clarke also thinks "winter" may describe stormy weather rather than the season. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/10-22.html
- **Hanukkah.** Today the festival is called Hanukkah or the Festival of Lights. It is not one of the festivals God gave through Moses, but the article says that doesn't make it displeasing to God. https://www.gotquestions.org/Feast-of-Dedication.html
- **Jesus attends a feast people created.** One older commentary on Bible Hub notes that though it was of human institution, our Lord did not scruple being present at it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries//john/10-22.htm
- **Timing.** Ellicott puts roughly two months between v. 21 and v. 22. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/10-22.html. John Piper says the same: about two months later than the Feast of Booths in John 7. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/i-and-the-father-are-one
- **An eyewitness detail.** The Cambridge Bible argues that naming this feast and the exact spot in v. 23 proclaim the eye-witness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries//john/10-22.htm
- **Winter as a picture.** Bible Hub's notes say "winter" also mirrors hearts growing cold in unbelief. https://biblehub.com/john/10-22.htm. Augustine (Catholic and Orthodox Church Father) made the same point: It was winter, and they were chill; because they were slow to approach that divine fire. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701048.htm

**v. 23**
- **Shelter.** Albert Barnes says the cold weather is given as a reason why he walked in Solomon's porch. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/10-22.html
- **The colonnade.** Matthew Henry says it was named for Solomon not because he built it, but because it stood where the porch bearing his name stood in the first temple. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/10-22.html. Meyer places it on the eastern side of the temple buildings. https://biblehub.com/commentaries//john/10-22.htm
- **Later use.** Acts 3:11 and 5:12 later place early believers there. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_is_John_10_22_s_feast_important.htm

**v. 24**
- **Their motive.** Augustine: They were not desiring the truth, but preparing a calumny. He adds that they probably only thought of the Christ in a human way. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701048.htm
- **Doubt.** Matthew Henry: Christ would make us to believe; we make ourselves doubt. https://biblehub.com/commentaries//john/10-22.htm

**vv. 25–26**
- **Not his sheep (Augustine).** He says people are sheep through believing, sheep in following the Shepherd. He reads "you are not of my sheep" to mean Jesus saw them predestined to everlasting destruction. He also urges his hearers: be ye sheep. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701048.htm
- **They understood.** Matthew Henry: The Jews understood his meaning, but could not form his words into a full charge against him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries//john/10-22.htm

**v. 27**
- **Following leads to life.** Bengel says following and the life (v. 28) are closely connected, comparing John 8:12. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/10-28.htm
- **Hearing and following (Wesleyan).** Adam Clarke makes Jesus' knowing and loving his sheep depend on their hearing and following. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rsv/john/10-28.html

**v. 28 – the main Protestant disagreement: can a true believer be lost?**
- **The shared reading.** "I give" is Not 'will give.' Several commentators treat eternal life as a gift the believer already has. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/10-28.htm. Barnes takes "perish" to mean future punishment and says Jesus' true disciples shall never be cast away. The word "pluck" means to seize as a robber takes his prey. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/10-28.htm
- **Reformed and Calvinist Baptist view.**
  - John Gill: the sheep were put in Christ's hands by the Father "from all eternity," when they were chosen in him. nor can any sin, or snare, or temptation, draw them out of Christ's hands. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/10-28.htm
  - Matthew Poole (Puritan): though believers may fall, they shall rise again by repentance. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/10-28.htm
  - Spurgeon: if one sheep could be snatched away, the devils would boast that Christ said that he would, but he could not. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/10-28.html
- **Wesleyan / Methodist view.** Adam Clarke: They who continue to hear Christ's voice, and to follow him, shall never perish. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rsv/john/10-28.html. He also rejects calling someone "one of the elect" who never perishes while he lives in sin. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/glt/john/10-28.html
- **Anglican view (Cambridge Bible).** It says the gift's retention depends on ourselves. The passage in no way asserts the indefectibility of the elect (that is, that the chosen cannot fall away). Christ's sheep cannot be taken from Him against their will; but their will is free, and they may choose to leave the flock. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/10-28.htm
- **The opposite argument from the Greek.**
  - Bengel (Lutheran Pietist) reads the Greek "perish" as reflexive: they shall not destroy themselves, internally. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/10-28.htm
  - A Blue Letter Bible blog post pushes this further. It concludes a true believer cannot, in any way, cause themselves to lose their salvation. https://blogs.blueletterbible.org/blb/2012/10/03/john-10-and-the-doctrine-of-eternal-security/
- **Constable (Dallas Seminary).** No one can snatch them: no thief (John 10:10), no robber (John 10:8), no wolf (John 10:12). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/10-28.html
- **Augustine (Catholic).** The wolf and thief destroy none but those predestined to destruction. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701048.htm

**v. 29**
- **Double safety.** Spurgeon: Jesus' people are kept by the Father's power. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/10-28.html. Piper: When you are in my hand, you are in his hand. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/i-and-the-father-are-one
- **A different Latin reading (Augustine).** Working from the wording "That which my Father gave me is greater than all," he takes the gift to be Jesus' Sonship itself: To be His own only-begotten Son. He reads "hand" as power: the power of Father and Son is one; for their Godhead is one. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701048.htm
- **Ryle (Anglican), quoted by Coffman.** Father and Son are one in essence, nature, dignity, power, will, and operation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/10-29.html

**v. 30**
- **The traditional reading.** David Guzik: "I and My Father" means two distinct Persons, which refutes the "Jesus Only" doctrine (anciently known as Sabelianism). That is the Oneness view that Father and Son are one Person. "One" is neuter in Greek, so it means one in essence, not one Person. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-10/
- **Against two old errors.** As Augustine and Bengel have said, the first clause is incompatible with Sabellianism, and the second clause with Arianism. Arianism held that the Son is a created being. https://biblehub.com/john/10-30.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary.** It calls this a oneness of redemptive power. https://biblehub.com/john/10-30.htm
- **Gill.** One "not in person" but in nature and essence, and perfections. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/10-30.html
- **Cautious readings.**
  - Barnes: the neuter word expresses union, but not the precise nature of the union. The kind of union must come from context, which here is protecting the sheep.
  - Constable: Jesus meant that He and the Father were one in their action.
  - Clarke (Methodist) asks whether Jesus could say this without blasphemy if he were not God.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/10-30.html
- **Preachers today.** Piper: the answer is way beyond messiahship. It is oneness with God the Father. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/i-and-the-father-are-one. John MacArthur: Jesus is claiming to be the divine Savior, the divine Redeemer, God of very God. https://www.gty.org/sermons/43-56/i-and-the-father-are-one-part-3

**v. 31**
- **The stones show what he meant.** Guzik says the charge of blasphemy proves that Jesus spoke of much more than a unity of purpose and will. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-10/
- **Augustine:** the Jews understood what the Arians understand not. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701048.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** the stones themselves "would speak it out." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_010.cfm

**vv. 32–33**
- **Jesus does not deny it.** Matthew Henry: they were right that Jesus was claiming to be God. Christ does not deny it, which he would have done if it had been a mistaken inference from his words. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_010.cfm
- **Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel):** They understood exactly what He was saying. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/10-29.html

**v. 34**
- **Who the "gods" are.**
  - Ellicott: "Law" means the whole Old Testament. In Psalm 82, God gives the name "gods" to the judges he appointed as representing Himself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/10-34.htm
  - Cambridge Bible: The argument is both à fortiori and ad hominem. In plain terms, it argues from the lesser to the greater, using the hearers' own Scripture. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/10-34.htm
  - Constable: the most likely view is Israel's judges as God's representatives; Another view is that these gods were angels. Gill notes that many Jewish writers took them as angels. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/10-34.html
- **Calvin:** Scripture gives the name of gods to those on whom God has conferred an honorable office. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/10-34.html
- **Catholic (Haydock):** the verse is about rulers who carry God's authority. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/10-34.html
- **Augustine (cited on Bible Hub):** humans are called "gods" by participation, whereas Christ is God by nature. https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_you_are_gods_in_John_10_34.htm
- **Debated modern teaching.**
  - Word of Faith: Bible Hub's article says the passage does not teach that humans are ontologically divine. It says Word of Faith claims that believers can "speak worlds into existence" misapply powers that belong to God alone. https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_you_are_gods_in_John_10_34.htm
  - Mormon (Latter-day Saint) use: Chuck Smith answers it, saying the verse simply declares the judges were called gods because of the responsibility they had of enacting God's judgments. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/10-34.html
  - MacArthur: "gods" here means gods with a small g, people who received God's delegated authority and his Word. https://www.gty.org/sermons/43-56/i-and-the-father-are-one-part-3

**v. 35**
- **From the lesser to the greater.** Matthew Henry: from the less to the greater. If they were gods, much more am I. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/10-34.html
- **Scripture cannot be broken.** Jesus argues that since Scripture calls those who received God's word "gods," calling himself Son of God can't be blasphemy. https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_you_are_gods_in_John_10_34.htm

**v. 36**
- **Sanctified and sent.** Guzik: This was a wonderful way for Jesus to speak of Himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-10/
- **Catholic (Haydock).** Jesus shows he is not God only in the sense the judges were. Augustine and others take "sanctified" as the eternal holiness the Son has from the Father. Others expound it of a greater sanctity and fulness of grace above all other saints, given to him, even as he was man. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/10-34.html

**vv. 37–38**
- **Two arguments.** Barnes says vv. 34–36 show they shouldn't object even if he were only a man. The second John 10:37-38 repeats substantially what he had before said, appealing to his works. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/web/john/10-34.html
- **Matthew Henry.**
  - The first argument only turned their own reasoning against them; in vv. 37–38 Jesus proves he and the Father are one.
  - In him dwelt all the fulness of the Godhead.
  - He knew the Father's mind not by communication, but by consciousness.
  - https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_010.cfm

**vv. 39–42**
- One commentary on Bible Hub sums up the section as Jesus escaping beyond the Jordan, Where Many Believe on Him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries//john/10-22.htm. I found no verse-by-verse comments on these verses in what I read.
